entries.name: GI DI Rushmore Parent LP v. Donald E. Stoops, Jr.

arguments_rejected_or_waived: Internal-affairs doctrine (Rushmore): rejected. Under Salzberg, forum-selection clauses can regulate intra-corporate claims, so disputes over them are intra-corporate claims rather than internal-affairs claims, and a choice-of-law analysis applies.

Delaware as the "default state" (Rushmore): rejected. The § 188 contacts favor Oklahoma: the place of contracting and the place of performance are Oklahoma, and negotiation, subject matter and domicile are neutral.

Place of performance is Delaware or neutral because Incentive Units sit in both states depending on vesting (Rushmore): rejected as confusing the place of performance with the location of the subject matter. The contract was performed by Stoops working for Bluepeak in Oklahoma.

No conflict between Delaware and Oklahoma law on forum-clause enforceability (Rushmore): rejected. Delaware typically enforces unnegotiated, otherwise-valid forum-selection clauses, while Oklahoma case law enforces only clauses the parties specifically negotiated or discussed.

Subject matter located in Oklahoma because the subject matter is Stoops's employment (Stoops): rejected. The subject matter is the grant of Incentive Units in return for work, so this factor is neutral (unvested units in Delaware, vested units in Oklahoma).

Court of Chancery's reliance on the Oklahoma Access Statute (Okla. Stat. tit. 15 § 216): not adopted (fn. 58). The statute preserves access to "ordinary tribunals," meaning a judicial forum rather than Oklahoma tribunals, so it does not embody a fundamental policy against forum-selection clauses. Gemini (Idaho statute requiring Idaho tribunals) does not compel a contrary reading.

Enforceability and reasonableness of the clause under Delaware law (Rushmore): not reached, because Oklahoma law governs. The Court of Chancery's alternative holding that lack of notice made enforcement unreasonable under Delaware law was neither reviewed nor endorsed.
Oklahoma's policy restricting non-competes: not reviewed. The Court limited its conflict review to forum-selection-clause enforcement.

authorities_cited.authority: Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws § 187(2)
authorities_cited.proposition: A contractual choice of law is enforced unless (a) there is no substantial relationship or other reasonable basis, or (b) applying it would contravene a fundamental policy of a state with a materially greater interest that would be the default state under § 188. The exceptions are disjunctive.

authorities_cited.authority: Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws § 188
authorities_cited.proposition: The default state is the state with the most significant relationship, evaluated through five contacts weighed by their relative importance to the dispute.

authorities_cited.authority: Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws § 187 cmt. g
authorities_cited.proposition: A fundamental policy may be embodied in a statute making contracts illegal or protecting against oppressive use of superior bargaining power. The Court extended this to policies embodied in case law.

authorities_cited.authority: Certain Underwriters at Lloyds, London v. Chemtura Corp., 160 A.3d 457 (Del. 2017)
authorities_cited.proposition: Choice-of-law determinations are reviewed de novo; Delaware follows the Restatement § 187 test, and the Restatement offers layers of guidance for identifying the most significant relationship.

authorities_cited.authority: Salzberg v. Sciabacucchi, 227 A.3d 102 (Del. 2020)
authorities_cited.proposition: Distinguishes internal corporate claims from broader intra-corporate claims, which forum provisions may regulate. The Court relied on it to hold that forum-selection disputes are intra-corporate claims subject to choice-of-law analysis.

authorities_cited.authority: Eads v. Woodmen of the World Life Ins. Soc'y, 785 P.2d 328 (Okla. Civ. App. 1989)
authorities_cited.proposition: Oklahoma's test for forum-selection clauses (the highest Oklahoma court to address the issue): lack of bargaining, a form contract, terms unreasonably favorable to one side, and unequal bargaining power can render a clause unreasonable.

authorities_cited.authority: Adams v. Bay Ltd., 60 P.3d 509 (Okla. Civ. App. 2002)
authorities_cited.proposition: Applies the Eads factors disjunctively; a clause not negotiated by the parties may be found invalid.

authorities_cited.authority: Howard Family Charitable Found., Inc. v. Trimble, 259 P.3d 850 (Okla. Civ. App. 2011)
authorities_cited.proposition: A disjunctive "unfair or unreasonable" standard may invalidate forum-selection clauses that the parties have not negotiated or discussed.

authorities_cited.authority: Burggraf Servs., Inc. v. H2O Solutions, 369 P.3d 52 (Okla. Civ. App. 2014)
authorities_cited.proposition: A forum-selection clause is unenforceable where there is no evidence it was negotiated and the defendants had relatively little bargaining power.

authorities_cited.authority: UBEO Holdings, LLC v. Drakulic, 2021 WL 1716966 (Del. Ch.); Mack v. Rev. Worldwide, Inc., 2020 WL 7774604 (Del. Ch. Dec. 30, 2020)
authorities_cited.proposition: Cited together: Delaware typically enforces unnegotiated, otherwise-valid forum-selection clauses, even where the party never read the agreement.

authorities_cited.authority: Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws § 188 cmt. e
authorities_cited.proposition: The place-of-negotiation contact is of less importance where there is no single place of negotiation.

authorities_cited.authority: Okla. Stat. tit. 15 § 216
authorities_cited.proposition: The Oklahoma Access Statute relied on below preserves access to ordinary (judicial) tribunals, not Oklahoma tribunals, and so is not a fundamental policy against forum-selection clauses (fn. 58).

authorities_cited.authority: Gemini Techs., Inc. v. Smith & Wesson Corp., 931 F.3d 911 (9th Cir. 2019)
authorities_cited.proposition: Construed an Idaho statute that expressly requires enforcement in Idaho tribunals, unlike Oklahoma's statute (fn. 58).

authorities_cited.authority: Edgar v. MITE Corp., 457 U.S. 624 (1982)
authorities_cited.proposition: The internal-affairs doctrine recognizes that only one state should regulate an entity's internal affairs.
Cited with Salzberg regarding internal corporate claims.

authorities_cited.authority: Focus Fin. Partners, LLC v. Holsopple, 241 A.3d 784 (Del. Ch. 2020)
authorities_cited.proposition: The § 188 contacts are evaluated according to their relative importance.

authorities_cited.authority: The Bremen v. Zapata Off-Shore Co., 407 U.S. 1 (1972)
authorities_cited.proposition: Quoted in Eads: the party resisting a forum clause may show the contractual forum is so gravely inconvenient as to deprive it of its day in court.

authorities_cited.authority: STI Trucking, LLC v. Santa Rosa Operating, LLC, 2021 WL 3604609 (N.D. Okla. Aug. 13, 2021)
authorities_cited.proposition: A forum-selection clause may be invalid where it was not negotiated or agreed upon.

authorities_cited.authority: CDX Holdings, Inc. v. Fox, 141 A.3d 1037 (Del. 2016)
authorities_cited.proposition: Factual findings are reviewed for clear error.

authorities_cited.authority: Sunder Energy, LLC v. Jackson, 332 A.3d 472 (Del. 2024)
authorities_cited.proposition: Preliminary injunction rulings are reviewed for abuse of discretion.

summary.brief_summary: Rushmore appealed the Court of Chancery's dismissal for lack of personal jurisdiction (GI DI Rushmore Parent L.P. v. Stoops, 2026 WL 1679305 (Del. Ch. June 10, 2026); the trial judge is not named in the order) of its suit to enforce restrictive covenants against Stoops, a former Bluepeak executive based in Oklahoma. The Court of Chancery held the Partnership Agreement's Delaware forum-selection clause unenforceable under both Oklahoma and Delaware law. The Supreme Court held that forum-clause disputes are intra-corporate rather than internal-affairs matters, that Oklahoma is the § 188 default state, and that Oklahoma case law's refusal to enforce unnegotiated forum clauses is a fundamental policy conflicting with Delaware law. Because the clause was never negotiated or discussed, Oklahoma would not enforce it, and the Court affirmed without reaching Delaware-law enforceability.
summary.core_legal_issue: Whether a Delaware forum-selection clause found only in a Delaware limited partnership agreement, which an Oklahoma-based employee joined through an incentive unit grant and joinder he signed without receiving or reading the partnership agreement, could supply personal jurisdiction over him in the Court of Chancery. The answer turned on whether the internal-affairs doctrine displaces choice-of-law analysis and, if not, whether Restatement (Second) § 187(2)(b) required applying Oklahoma law, under which unnegotiated forum-selection clauses are unenforceable.
summary.holding: Affirmed: the dismissal for lack of personal jurisdiction and the denial of the preliminary injunction. The internal-affairs doctrine does not govern because, under Salzberg, forum-selection disputes are intra-corporate claims, so a choice-of-law analysis applies. Under Restatement § 187(2)(b), Oklahoma is the default state under § 188. A fundamental policy may be embodied in case law as well as statute, and Oklahoma case law in the Eads line treats lack of negotiation of a forum-selection clause as sufficient to void it. That conflicts with Delaware's typical enforcement of unnegotiated clauses, so Oklahoma law governs the Partnership Agreement's forum-selection clause. Because the clause was undisputedly neither negotiated nor discussed (Stoops never received the Partnership Agreement before signing the Joinder), the Court predicted Oklahoma would not enforce it. Without the clause, Delaware lacks personal jurisdiction over Stoops. The Court affirmed on Oklahoma case law rather than the Court of Chancery's Access Statute rationale, which it found does not establish a fundamental policy against forum clauses (fn. 58). It did not decide whether Delaware law would enforce the clause.
key_facts_and_concessions: The Partnership Agreement's forum-selection clause was Rushmore's only asserted basis for personal jurisdiction, below and on appeal. Stoops is an Oklahoma resident with no Delaware contacts, and neither party argued any other basis.

When Stoops signed the Unit Agreement and the Joinder Agreement, he had neither received nor read the Partnership Agreement, despite acknowledging in Unit Agreement § 7.7 that he had, and he had not asked for it. He first requested it in February 2024, more than two and a half years later.
It was undisputed that Stoops and Rushmore did not negotiate or discuss the forum-selection clause.
Only the Partnership Agreement contains the Delaware forum-selection clause; both the Unit Agreement and the Partnership Agreement contain Delaware choice-of-law provisions.

Stoops lived and worked in Oklahoma for his entire Bluepeak tenure (Vice President, Market Development, June 2021 to April 2026) and signed the Unit Agreement there. Rushmore agreed that Oklahoma is the place of contracting (Reply Br. at 12).
The parties negotiated the Unit Agreement minimally and from separate states.

The Unit Agreement granted Incentive Units (about 2% of Rushmore's management incentive pool) in consideration for Stoops's services. It made him a limited partner and imposed four restrictive covenants: non-competition, non-solicitation and confidentiality for two years post-employment, and non-disparagement in perpetuity.

Rushmore sued after Stoops resigned to join Dobson Fiber, a Bluepeak competitor, seeking injunctions and damages for breach of the covenants. Bluepeak (Clarity Telecom, LLC) is a Delaware LLC and Rushmore's only subsidiary.
summary.practical_takeaway: Sponsors that grant equity to out-of-state employees should not rely on a forum-selection clause buried in an unseen partnership agreement incorporated by joinder. Put the clause in the signed grant document, deliver the governing agreement before signing, and document any negotiation or discussion of the clause, because the Supreme Court will apply the employee's home-state law where its case law embodies a fundamental policy. Plaintiffs should also develop any independent basis for personal jurisdiction rather than resting solely on the clause.
summary.standard_of_review: De novo for choice-of-law determinations in contract disputes; clear error for factual findings; abuse of discretion for the grant or denial of a preliminary injunction.

arguments_rejected_or_waived: Rule 12(b)(7) failure to join the Stevenson Trust: rejected. The validity of the May 2024 assignment is fact-intensive and turns on Section 13, Respondent's account of it is a factual injection (fn. 45), and the Trust has notice through Ms. Stevenson as Trustee and may intervene if necessary.

Forum non conveniens dismissal: rejected. Rancho Verde is a Delaware LLC, § 18-802 relief belongs in this Court, the Operating Agreement selects Delaware law and forum and waives venue objections, no foreign law is at issue, the California Action involves different parties, and nothing shows it has decided any preclusive issue (fn. 51).

Stay in favor of the California Action under McWane and Doehler: rejected. Respondent failed to contend meaningfully with Purchase Agreement § 7.12's arbitration clause, which raises concerns that deferring to the California Action would be inappropriate, so Respondent overstated Doehler's support for a stay.

Failure to plead deadlock (including the Petition's internal inconsistency): rejected. Under either alternative ownership theory a deadlock is reasonably conceivable because §§ 8 and 12(a) are ambiguous and require extrinsic evidence.

Manufactured deadlock (Petitioner contracted to sell, then raced to this Court instead of performing): rejected. The Court could not find the deadlock manufactured on a motion-to-dismiss record, given the alleged deterioration of the Members' relationship and failed buyout efforts.
Doehler compels dismissal and the Petitioner's distinctions are only alternative grounds: rejected. Unlike Doehler, no contractual mechanism is unambiguously available to break the impasse.

The Company still performs its sole purpose of holding the Property, with Ms. Stevenson running daily operations as Managing Member: rejected. Purpose is not the crux of the dispute, the effect of her Managing Member role is ambiguous, and an impasse over even basic decisions to care for the Property is alleged.
Lesser relief suffices: the Court could not conclude, given the conflicting provisions, that the alleged facts require less drastic relief than dissolution.
Petitioner's request for leave to amend or supplement: unnecessary because the motion is denied.
Custodian and accounting counts: the Court did not analyze them in depth because Respondent's arguments failed for the reasons given (fn. 117).

authorities_cited.proposition: Authorizes judicial dissolution of a Delaware LLC; the basis for the Court's subject-matter jurisdiction and for the claim found adequately pleaded.

authorities_cited.authority: Rancho Verde, LLC Operating Agreement §§ 2, 8, 12(a), 13, 16, 21, 24
authorities_cited.proposition: Unanimity for additional capital contributions, a conditional Managing Member designation within a member-managed structure, consent requirements for assignments, and Delaware governing-law, forum and venue-waiver provisions.

authorities_cited.authority: Purchase Agreement § 7.12 (Dkt. 8 Ex. C)
authorities_cited.proposition: The arbitration clause raised concerns that deferring to the California Action would be inappropriate.

authorities_cited.authority: In re Seneca Invs. LLC, 970 A.2d 259 (Del. Ch. 2008)
authorities_cited.proposition: Dissolution has been ordered where deadlock prevented the entity from operating or its purpose was fulfilled or impossible; conclusory allegations are not accepted.

authorities_cited.authority: In re Silver Leaf, L.L.C., 2005 WL 2045641 (Del. Ch. Aug. 18, 2005)
authorities_cited.proposition: Dissolution is appropriate where majority action is needed for important matters and the agreement provides no mechanism to break the impasse.

authorities_cited.authority: Kahn v. Portnoy, 2008 WL 5197164 (Del. Ch. Dec. 11, 2008)
authorities_cited.proposition: An ambiguity in an LLC agreement cannot be resolved on a motion to dismiss; dissolution is available where management is so dysfunctional, as in voting deadlock, that operating is no longer practicable.

authorities_cited.authority: Salamone v. Gorman, 106 A.3d 354 (Del. 2014)
authorities_cited.proposition: Extrinsic evidence may be considered where a contract is susceptible to more than one reasonable interpretation.

authorities_cited.authority: Holzbaur v. Trolley Square Hosp., LLC, 340 A.3d 603 (Del. Ch. 2025)
authorities_cited.proposition: Two conflicting provisions render a contract ambiguous.

authorities_cited.authority: Banks v. Banks, 2007 WL 135638 (Del. Ch. Jan. 11, 2007)
authorities_cited.proposition: A Rule 12(b)(7) determination is fact-intensive; the Court considers whether the absent party has been informed of the action.

authorities_cited.authority: Troy Corp. v. Schoon, 2007 WL 949441 (Del. Ch. Mar. 26, 2007)
authorities_cited.proposition: On Rule 12(b)(3) the Court may consider extrinsic evidence; courts give effect to contractual forum designations.

authorities_cited.authority: Martinez v. E.I. DuPont de Nemours & Co., 86 A.3d 1102 (Del. 2014)
authorities_cited.proposition: Forum non conveniens is discretionary; a defendant's interest in having foreign-law issues decided by courts whose law governs is not implicated here.

authorities_cited.authority: In re Coinmint, LLC, 261 A.3d 867 (Del. Ch. 2021)
authorities_cited.proposition: Section 18-802 applies only to Delaware LLCs; the Court has an ongoing duty to assess subject-matter jurisdiction.

authorities_cited.authority: In re Doehler Dry Ingredient Sols., LLC, 2022 WL 4281841 (Del. Ch. Sept. 15, 2022), aff'd, 294 A.3d 64 (Del. 2023)
authorities_cited.proposition: Dismissal of a deadlock dissolution petition where the deadlock was prospective or manufactured and remediable through a mechanism within the operating agreement; no such mechanism is unambiguously available here.

authorities_cited.authority: McWane Cast Iron Pipe Corp. v. McDowell-Wellman Eng'g Co., 263 A.2d 281 (Del. 1970)
authorities_cited.proposition: Respondent's basis for a stay in favor of the California Action, rejected given the Purchase Agreement's arbitration clause.

authorities_cited.authority: Haley v. Talcott, 864 A.2d 86 (Del. Ch. 2004)
authorities_cited.proposition: Dissolution was ordered on summary judgment for indisputable deadlock between two 50% members.

authorities_cited.authority: Fisk Ventures LLC v. Segal, 2009 WL 73957 (Del. Ch. Jan. 13, 2009)
authorities_cited.proposition: Quoted through Doehler: a deadlock remediable through a mechanism within the operating agreement.

authorities_cited.authority: Hassanein v. NTO Fund I, 2026 WL 2240127 (Del. Ch. Aug. 4, 2026)
authorities_cited.proposition: A provision authorizing a manager to manage an LLC does not alter a unanimity requirement.
Standard for required parties.

authorities_cited.authority: Cent. Mortg. Co. v. Morgan Stanley Mortg. Cap. Hldgs. LLC, 27 A.3d 531 (Del. 2011)
authorities_cited.proposition: Rule 12(b)(6) reasonable conceivability standard.

authorities_cited.authority: Malpiede v. Townson, 780 A.2d 1075 (Del. 2001)
authorities_cited.proposition: Cited for when a document is a matter outside the pleading; the Operating Agreement, referenced in the Petition, was treated as within it.
Alternative remedial paths for LLC governance disputes.

authorities_cited.authority: Ct. Ch. R. 144
authorities_cited.proposition: The letter is not a final report, so exceptions are stayed.

summary.brief_summary: The Diamos Irrevocable Trust petitioned under 6 Del. C. § 18-802 to dissolve Rancho Verde, LLC, a two-member Delaware LLC holding California real property, and Respondent Tracy Stevenson moved to dismiss or stay, invoking non-joinder of the Stevenson Trust, forum non conveniens in favor of a later-filed California action to enforce a purchase of Petitioner's interest, and failure to plead deadlock. The Magistrate in Chancery denied the motion in a non-final letter report, finding that each argument injected factual disputes, including the validity of the May 2024 assignment and whether the deadlock was manufactured, that cannot be resolved on the pleadings. The Court found deadlock adequately pleaded because the Operating Agreement's unanimity requirement for capital contributions and its conditional Managing Member designation are ambiguous, and it distinguished Doehler because no deadlock-breaking mechanism is unambiguously available here. The Court declined a stay given the Delaware forum and venue-waiver provisions and the Purchase Agreement's arbitration clause.
summary.core_legal_issue: Whether a 6 Del. C. § 18-802 petition to dissolve a two-member Delaware LLC whose sole asset is California real property should be dismissed or stayed for failure to join the Stevenson Trust (alleged assignee of Respondent's interest), for forum non conveniens in favor of a later-filed California action to enforce a purchase of Petitioner's interest, or for failure to plead a deadlock, where the Operating Agreement's capital-contribution and management provisions are ambiguous.

flags.assertion: as a Magistrate's report the ruling is not binding until adopted
flags.evidence: I find the Court has subject-matter jurisdiction... This is not a final report under Court of Chancery Rule 144 and exceptions are stayed.
flags.opinion_says: The opinion matches each element of the summary except the added statement that the ruling is not binding until adopted, which it never says; it says only that the report is not final and exceptions are stayed.
flags.problem: The opinion does not say the ruling is non-binding until adopted; it states only that it is not a final report and exceptions are stayed.

summary.holding: The Magistrate in Chancery denied Respondent's motion to dismiss under Rules 12(b)(1), (3), (6) and (7) and the alternative request for a stay; as a Magistrate's report the ruling is not binding until adopted. The Court found subject-matter jurisdiction because the Petition seeks § 18-802 relief as to a Delaware LLC. It held that whether the Stevenson Trust is a required party turns on the disputed validity of the May 2024 assignment under Section 13, and that the Trust has notice through its trustee and may intervene. It rejected forum non conveniens and a stay given the Operating Agreement's Delaware law, forum and venue-waiver provisions, the different parties in the California Action, and the Purchase Agreement's arbitration clause. On the merits, the Court held deadlock reasonably conceivable under either of the Petition's alternative ownership theories, because § 8 (unanimity for additional contributions) and § 12(a) (conditional Managing Member within a member-managed structure) conflict and are ambiguous, requiring extrinsic evidence. Unlike in Doehler, no contractual deadlock-breaking mechanism is unambiguously available, and whether the deadlock was manufactured cannot be decided on this record. The letter is not a final report under Rule 144, and exceptions are stayed.
key_facts_and_concessions: Petitioner and Ms. Stevenson are alleged to be Rancho Verde's only Members; each contributed about $108,000 toward the Property, and Petitioner later funded about $225,000 more in expenditures and improvements. The Petition pleads in the alternative that this gave Petitioner a majority interest or that the Members hold equal shares.

Operating Agreement § 8 bars additional Capital Contributions without "consent or approval of all Members"; the Petition pleads no facts showing whether Respondent consented to or approved the $225,000.

Operating Agreement § 12(a) makes the Company member-managed, but names Ms. Stevenson Managing Member "until all members designate otherwise" and allows majority-interest action except where unanimity is required. The Court found these provisions conflicting and ambiguous.

Respondent's Ex. B shows Ms. Stevenson assigned her interest to the Stevenson Trust in May 2024; the Stevenson Trust is not named. Section 13 requires consent of the non-assigning majority, and nothing on the face of Ex. B suggests Petitioner reviewed or approved it.

Four days after the Petition was filed, the Stevenson Trust sued in Placer County, California to enforce a purchase agreement for Petitioner's interest; Purchase Agreement § 7.12 requires neutral, binding arbitration of disputes not settled by mediation.
Operating Agreement §§ 21 and 24 select Delaware law, give Delaware state and federal courts non-exclusive jurisdiction, and waive any objection to venue there.
The Petition alleges the Members cannot agree on recognition of Petitioner's additional capital contributions, a buyout, sale of the Property, or ongoing management of the Company.

Petitioner did not attach the Operating Agreement; the Court used Respondent's Dkt. 8 Ex. A, which Petitioner itself cited as the operative agreement, so its operative status was treated as undisputed (fn. 1).
summary.practical_takeaway: Respondents seeking early dismissal of a § 18-802 deadlock petition should expect contested assignments, manufactured-deadlock theories and internally conflicting governance provisions to be treated as fact questions, and should not rely on Doehler without an unambiguous deadlock-breaking mechanism in the LLC agreement. A party seeking a stay in favor of a foreign action must confront any arbitration clause in the contract underlying that action.
summary.standard_of_review: Ct. Ch. R. 12(b)(6) reasonable conceivability (well-pleaded facts accepted as true, reasonable inferences drawn for the non-movant, conclusory allegations not accepted); Rule 12(b)(3), under which the Court may consider extrinsic evidence from the outset and forum non conveniens is addressed to the trial court's discretion; Rule 12(b)(7)/Rule 19(a)(1) required-party analysis; Rule 12(b)(1) subject-matter jurisdiction.
